sentences.text: Bungartius was an extinct joint-necked fish that lived in Ohio during the Late Devonian period. This mid-sized arthrodire possessed a cranial shield measuring exactly 40.5 cm in length.
It stands as the only known member of its family, Bungartiidae, and is related to the giant fish Titanichthys.
The dorsal body armor was short, low, and narrow, resembling the shape of its skull.
Its lower jaw plates were large and lacked cusps, ending in a short, downward-inclined tip. Thickened shearing surfaces on this jaw suggest the animal was adapted for crushing hard prey.

The first specimen was found by Peter A. Bungart in Cuyahuga County, Ohio, within the Cleveland Shale Member of the Ohio Shale. In 1936, Peter Anthony Bungart recovered a concretion containing dorsal and ventral armor plates from the same location.
David H. Dunkle formally described the genus and species Bungartius perissus in 1947.

Researchers suggest that Bungartius may have been a durophage, feeding on hard-shelled invertebrates. Thickened shearing surfaces on the lower jaw support the idea that it was adapted for crushing hard prey.
The spinal plates in front of the pectoral fin attachment were completely atrophied, and the postero-lateral plates have not yet been identified.
In 1975, Robert Howland Denison classified Bungartius into its own family, Bungartiidae.
Robert Howland Denison suggested that the family Bungartiidae belonged to the clade Pachyosteina, which included dominant placoderms of the Upper Devonian.
A 2017 phylogenetic analysis placed Bungartius as an intermediate form between Tafilalichthys and Titanichthys.
Bungartius lived during the Famennian stage, between 365.2 and 358.86 million years ago.
